chapter: Caravan, Perdido and the first tunes
title: Perdido's success and late payments from Tempo
summary: Tizol says Perdido and Caravan were his best tunes and he was shortchanged on royalties; he and Rose complain that Tempo, run by Duke's sister, pays late.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: have no business getting nothing, but later on in the years, he gave me a percentage on Caravan, which has been the two best things for me -- that was Caravan and Perdifo. And that old sonofabitch, that sister of Duke Ellington, you know -- she was the one who messed me up.
How?

Well, I still got some. No, because I didn't get any money, and I should have got some. Because I went one time over here to Sunset and Vine at this store where they sell records, and the man showed me in the book, Perdifo was two and three pages. Not only by our band, but by every band -- because one time, Perdifo was the best jazz tune at that particular time. And you could hear it on the radio, every five minutes, some other band would be playing "Perdifo." It was the biggest jazz tune at that particular time.
Was it published by Tempo?
Yeah.
And, what? You didn't get your royalties from Tempo, is that it?
I got some, but I didn't get what I should have gotten.
And they don't ever pay on time.
Okay, baby doll.
They don't ever pay on time.
Right now they owe me the second payment.
I still haven't gotten it; it should have been two months ago, and I haven't gotten no money yet from Ruth. hasn't even gotten
He got the first payment, and the AGAC said they are always late. Ruth hates to pay her bills.
I heard that they were bankrupt, but we found out they are not bankrupt. Had you heard anything about it?

I didn't hear they were bankrupt; I heard she was selling a few things -- Louie told me, oh, I forget what it was he wanted to do, but he had some tunes that were in Tempo, and I guess he called about them or something, and he found out that they're not with Tempo any more. She sold them to some other publisher. I guess she's selling off a few things at a time; I don't know.
The auditors were in there, you know.
I don't know.
Yeah, they were. I know that to be a fact.
I know Irving Mills wanted to buy it from her, but ...
Robinson one time asked me to, and asked Duke Ellington -- how about "Perdido" and "Backkiff," and I said, "I put my signature, you write the amount for them." I told Duke, "What are you doing?"
And they don't pay their bills.

But I called up AGAC, and when that check doesn't come here, I call AGAC, and I tell them and they call New York, and the man told AGAC, he said, "She's late as usual." They are always late, and when Duke Ellington was living, Juan used to call Duke, and would say, "Duke, where is my check?" He, in turn, would call Ruth and we would get the money. But now that Duke's gone ... and all publishers know that she is a terrible payer.
Well, I think it's kind of disorganized at Tempo. She said that Stevie and Michael are running it for her, but I don't know.
Nobody's running it.
Who is running Tempo now?
Well, she said ...
What did you hear from?

Irving Mills had me call her a year or so ago, and ask her if she was interested in selling Tempo, so I called her and she said, or I said, he wanted to talk to her and she said that, sure, she'd talk to him. So I said what are Stevie and Michael doing, and she said they were running Tempo.
Stevie and Michael are her sons?
Right, uh huh.
Nobody's running it. Truthfully. It's running itself.
Wait Rose; take it easy.
